title: LFSR: patterns made on chip
summary: The heart of almost every BIST pattern generator is the **linear feedback shift register (LFSR)**: a few flip-flops and XOR gates that step through a long, random-looking but fully repeatable sequence of patterns.
objectives: Build a Fibonacci LFSR and compute its next states by hand.
Explain the Galois form and why it is faster.
Explain primitive polynomials, maximal length 2ⁿ − 1 and the all-zero lock-up state.
Explain why LFSR patterns are useful as test patterns.

blocks.md: Take a shift register of 4 flip-flops, Q1 → Q2 → Q3 → Q4. On every clock edge each bit moves one place to the right. Now **feed back** into Q1 the XOR of some of the outputs — here Q3 and Q4. This is a **Fibonacci LFSR**:

blocks.alt: 4-bit Fibonacci LFSR with feedback Q3 XOR Q4 into Q1
blocks.caption: Four flip-flops and one XOR gate

blocks.md:
The rule for the next state is simple:

- new **Q1** = Q3 ⊕ Q4 (the feedback)
- new **Q2** = old Q1, new **Q3** = old Q2, new **Q4** = old Q3

Start it with the **seed** 1000 and step through the clocks:

steps.title: Clock 0 — seed 1000
steps.md: Q3 ⊕ Q4 = 0 ⊕ 0 = **0**. On the next edge 0 enters Q1 and everything shifts right.

steps.title: Clock 2 — 0010
steps.md: Now Q3 = 1: Q3 ⊕ Q4 = 1 ⊕ 0 = **1** → a 1 enters Q1: next state 1001.

steps.title: Clock 7 — 0101
steps.md: Q3 ⊕ Q4 = 0 ⊕ 1 = **1** → 1010 … and so on. After **15** clocks the register is back at 1000.

blocks.caption: The complete sequence: all 15 non-zero states, then it repeats

blocks.title: Only 4 flip-flops and 1 XOR
blocks.md: This tiny circuit produces 15 different patterns without any memory. A 32-bit LFSR with 4 taps produces over **4 billion** patterns before it repeats.
There is a second way to build an LFSR. Instead of collecting many outputs into one XOR at the input, the last output Q4 is sent back and **XORed into the shift path** between stages:
All taps meet in **one XOR tree** that drives Q1. With many taps the tree has several levels of XOR gates — a long path.

Q4 goes back to Q1 **and** into a 2-input XOR placed in front of Q4. Rule: new Q1 = Q4, new Q2 = Q1, new Q3 = Q2, new Q4 = Q3 ⊕ Q4. Started from 1000 it also runs through **all 15** non-zero states, in a different order: 1000, 0100, 0010, 0001, 1001, 1101, 1111, …

rows: one XOR tree at the input
grows with the number of taps
blocks.caption: Same family, different wiring

blocks.md:
Which taps should we use? Every LFSR is described by a **characteristic polynomial**. The exponents tell where the taps are. Our first LFSR uses taps Q4 and Q3, so its polynomial is

> p(x) = x⁴ + x³ + 1

An n-bit register has 2ⁿ states. One of them — **all zeros** — is special: 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, so the register stays at 0000 forever. That leaves at most **2ⁿ − 1** states in the cycle. An LFSR that visits all of them is called **maximal-length**, and it is maximal-length exactly when its polynomial is **primitive**.

tabs.label: Primitive: x⁴ + x³ + 1
tabs.md: Taps Q4, Q3. From **any** non-zero seed the register runs through **all 15** non-zero states before it repeats. Good for test: no state is missed.

tabs.label: Not primitive: x⁴ + x² + 1
tabs.md:
Taps Q4, Q2. The 15 non-zero states split into **three short cycles**:

- 1000 → 0100 → 1010 → 0101 → 0010 → 0001 → (6 states)
- 1001 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → (6 states)
- 1011 → 1101 → 0110 → (3 states)

Which cycle you get depends on the seed — and most patterns are **never** produced. Bad for test.

blocks.title: The lock-up state
blocks.md: Never seed an XOR-based LFSR with all zeros — it will stay at zero forever. BIST controllers load a non-zero seed at reset, and some designs add a little logic to escape from 0…0.

blocks.caption: Some primitive polynomials (Fibonacci taps: XOR the outputs of these stages into Q1)

blocks.md: You do not need to find primitive polynomials yourself — tables for every length up to hundreds of bits are published. Note that some lengths (like 8) need **four** taps; no two-tap primitive polynomial exists for them.

The **seed** is the state the LFSR starts from. Because the next state depends only on the current state, the same seed always gives **exactly the same sequence**. The patterns look random, but they are fully **repeatable** — that is why they are called **pseudo-random**.

items.title: Why repeatable matters
items.md: The expected responses of the circuit can be computed once by simulation. Every chip, in the factory or in a car years later, runs the **same** patterns and must give the **same** result (the *golden signature*, Topic 5).

items.title: Why random-looking matters
items.md: Neighbouring bits are hardly related, ones and zeros are balanced (a maximal-length sequence has 2ⁿ⁻¹ ones and 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 zeros), and many different combinations reach the logic quickly. For many circuits, a few thousand random patterns already detect most stuck-at faults.

items.title: Exhaustive test of small blocks
items.md: An n-bit maximal-length LFSR applies **every** non-zero n-bit pattern. For a block with few inputs this is an exhaustive test: all input combinations except 0…0 (which can be added with a little extra logic).

items.title: Why not just a counter?
items.md: A binary counter also visits all states, but its low bits toggle all the time and its high bits almost never — the patterns are strongly correlated. It also needs an adder chain, while an LFSR needs only a few XORs.

blocks.prompt: Practice: a 3-bit LFSR has feedback Q2 ⊕ Q3 into Q1. Put its first states in order, starting from the seed 100.

questions.text: The 4-bit LFSR of this topic (new Q1 = Q3 ⊕ Q4, then shift right) is in state Q1Q2Q3Q4 = **1101**. What is the next state?
questions.explain: Q3 ⊕ Q4 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1 enters Q1; the old Q1Q2Q3 = 110 move right → **1110**.

questions.text: A 5-bit LFSR has a primitive polynomial. How many different states does it go through before repeating?
questions.explain: Maximal length is 2⁵ − 1 = **31**: every state except all zeros.

questions.text: Why must an LFSR never be started with the all-zero seed?
options: The XOR of zeros is zero, so the register stays at 0…0 forever.
All-zero is not allowed in SystemVerilog.
The flip-flops cannot store zeros after reset.
It would produce the sequence in reverse order.

questions.text: Any choice of taps gives an n-bit LFSR that visits all 2ⁿ − 1 non-zero states.
questions.explain: Only a **primitive** polynomial gives maximal length. x⁴ + x² + 1, for example, splits into cycles of 6, 6 and 3 states.

questions.text: What is the main advantage of the Galois form over the Fibonacci form?
options: Only a single 2-input XOR lies between any two flip-flops, so it can run faster.
It produces a longer sequence for the same number of flip-flops.
It can start from the all-zero state.

questions.text: A 3-bit LFSR has new Q1 = Q2 ⊕ Q3. Put the first five states in order, starting from the seed 100.
Why is an LFSR a good BIST pattern generator? Select **all** correct answers.
options: It needs only a few flip-flops and XOR gates.
The same seed always gives the same sequence.
Its patterns look random and reach many combinations quickly.
It produces every pattern including all zeros without extra logic.
